key_insight: Microscopic residual impurities in wide-bandgap perovskite films act as degradation nucleation sites, and can be rapidly detected with microscopy plus machine learning before devices fail.
engineering_relevance: The work provides a fast, non-invasive pre-screening tool for scaling perovskite solar-cell manufacturing by flagging films with high early-stage instability risk.
method: Nano-FTIR to chemically identify impurity phases
High-resolution reflected-light microscopy for fast, non-invasive imaging
Machine learning image analysis to quantify impurity density in seconds
evidence_signal: Photo-stress and degradation-tracking experiments showed that degradation starts at impurity–perovskite interfaces, and films with higher impurity density degraded faster early on.
watch_item: The diagnostic depends on a chemically validated imaging pipeline and may need calibration across different perovskite compositions, processing routes, and microscope setups.
paper_title: High-Throughput Imaging of Degradation-Inducing Microscopic Impurities in Perovskite Solar Cells
